lesson.title: Richtung I: links, rechts, geradeaus, oben, unten
lesson.subtitle: left, right, and the words that point the way — one twin, one loner, three builders

hook.title: Left Is the Loner
hook.content: Two of today's five are twins; three are builders. rechts is right — the same ancient word *rehtaz, 'straight, correct', which is why direction and correctness are one idea in both languages (du hast recht / you are right — you already own the adjective). English kept the -ight family — right, light, night, eight — and German answers with -echt and -acht: recht, Licht, Nacht, acht. One photo album, two spellings. links is the honest loner: no English twin survives. English's own left grew from a different old word meaning 'weak', and the two never were related — some twins simply die, and pretending otherwise is how etymology gets a bad name. geradeaus is two small words welded: gerade ('straight') + aus ('out') — straight-out, the whole direction in one breath. And oben and unten are the adverbs of prepositions you already trust: oben is built on über's root (über ↔ over), unten on unter's (unter ↔ under). Up is over's adverb; down is under's.

footnotes.title: The Adverbial -s
footnotes.content: rechts, links — and morgens, abends — all wear an old genitive -s: 'of the right', 'of the morning'. English once marked adverbs the same way and keeps the fossil in 'besides' and the old phrase 'needs must'. The -s is not a plural and not a verb ending; it is grammar's dust.

pattern.title: Which Way? One Word Each
pattern.content: 1. Sideways: nach links, nach rechts — Die Kirche ist links, das Auto steht rechts. 2. Ahead: Gehen Sie geradeaus — and the street's own answer, Immer geradeaus! 3. Vertical: Der Himmel ist oben, der Garten ist unten. 4. Living there: Oben wohnen sechs Familien. 5. With a walk: Gehen Sie fünf Minuten geradeaus. 6. Home at last: Endlich bin ich zu Hause. The words never inflect — no endings, no agreement; they sit where adverbs sit and point where you face.
pattern.linguist_note: Unlike the months, the direction words are pure Germanic — no Latin ever planted a flag on the body's own map. Left and right are anchored to your facing hand, up and down to your height, which is why every language inherits the same body-relative frame and fills it with its own sounds.

exercises.prompt: Directions in place — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The church is on the left
The car is on the right
We live here — the church is over there
matching_pairs.german: Wir wohnen hier — die Kirche ist drüben

matching_pairs.english: The car is parked over there

exercises.target_answer: Die Kirche ist links, Das Auto steht rechts, Gehen Sie geradeaus, Der Himmel ist oben, Der Garten ist unten, Oben wohnen sechs Familien, Endlich bin ich zu Hause, Wir wohnen hier — die Kirche ist drüben, Das Auto steht dort
exercises.meaning: left, right, straight ahead, up, down
exercises.explanation: One word per direction, no prepositions, no endings. And the vertical pair stays busy: oben wohnen sechs Familien — upstairs, where the families are — while der Garten waits unten.

exercises.prompt: links has no English twin — but its partner does. Give the English twin of rechts:
exercises.meaning: rechts ↔ right — the true pair; links is the honest loner
exercises.explanation: rechts and right are the same word *rehtaz — the -ight/-echt family with light/Licht and night/Nacht. links never had an English twin: English's left grew from an old word meaning 'weak'. Honest limitation, not a missed connection.

exercises.prompt: You already know 'du hast recht' (you are right). Which word is the DIRECTION twin of that recht?
exercises.meaning: rechts is the adverb of recht — direction and correctness are one root
exercises.explanation: English did the same thing with one word: right (correct) and right (not left). German split the jobs — recht keeps the meaning, rechts takes the direction — but both grow from *rehtaz, 'straight'. The straight path and the correct answer are the same idea.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the walking direction: 'Go five minutes straight ahead'
exercises.explanation: The verb leads, Sie follows, the measure of time sits in the middle, and geradeaus closes the sentence — the same slot the duration accusative took with dauern. Swap fünf for sechs and the walk gets longer.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'Sometimes I go left and sometimes right'
exercises.target_answer: Manchmal gehe ich nach links und manchmal nach rechts
exercises.meaning: Sometimes I go left and sometimes right
exercises.explanation: manchmal opens the sentence and pushes gehe to slot 2 — the V2 swap again. nach is the pointing preposition: nach links, nach rechts, nach Hause. The repetition is the rhythm of real street directions.

summary.outcome: Point all five ways — links, rechts, geradeaus, oben, unten — and know which twin lives, which died, and which are compounds.

use_example.german: Gehen Sie geradeaus — die Kirche ist links, wir wohnen oben.
use_example.english: Go straight ahead — the church is on the left, we live upstairs.

summary.takeaway: rechts/right is one word (*rehtaz, with recht, Licht, Nacht, acht), links has no English twin, geradeaus is gerade+aus, and oben/unten are the adverbs of über/over and unter/under.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: hinten and the compass — Norden, Osten, Westen, Süden — the map the sun drew.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Richtung I: links, rechts, geradeaus, oben, unten (Sometimes I go left and sometimes right):
twist.target_answer: Manchmal gehe ich nach links und manchmal nach rechts
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Manchmal gehe ich nach links und manchmal nach rechts" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Richtung I: links, rechts, geradeaus, oben, unten without relying on short-term echo.

links.context_translation: The bank is on the left.
links.etymology_derivation: Middle High German linkes; only Dutch links is a cognate — no English cognate, memorize this one. [wiktionary]

rechts.context_translation: The car is on the right.
rechts.etymology_derivation: recht + adverbial -s; recht is the direct cognate of English right (Recht, already known). [wiktionary]

geradeaus.context_phrase: Gehen Sie geradeaus bis zur Ecke.
geradeaus.context_translation: Go straight ahead to the corner.
geradeaus.etymology_derivation: gerade + aus fused into one adverb; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

oben.context_phrase: Das Buch ist oben auf dem Tisch.
oben.context_translation: The book is up on the table.
oben.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ubanē, kin to über (over); no direct English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

unten.etymology_derivation: Old High German undenân, kin to unter (under); no direct English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

hier.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hēr — the explicit cognate of English here. [wiktionary]

drüben.context_translation: The post office is over there.
drüben.etymology_derivation: From a rare üben, a variant of über formed by the analogy of unter/unten and ober/oben — literally over yonder; über is the twin of over. [wiktionary]

familie.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin familia — the same Latin source as English family. [wiktionary]

wohnen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wunāną, from the 'wish, love' root; no English cognate named on Wiktionary. [wiktionary]

auto.etymology_derivation: Short for Automobil — the same Greek autos ('self') loan as English auto, clipped German-style. [wiktionary]

kirche.etymology_derivation: Greek kyriakon → Scottish kirk / German Kirche.

garten.context_translation: The children play in the garden.

fünf.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *fimf, PIE *pénkʷe — the twin of English five. [wiktionary]

sechs.context_translation: It is six o'clock in the morning.
sechs.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *sehs, PIE *swéḱs — the same root as English six. [wiktionary]

manchmal.context_translation: Sometimes I go to the cinema.
manchmal.etymology_derivation: manch (many a) + Mal (time, the meal-word cousin) — 'many a time'. [wiktionary]

endlich.etymology_derivation: Ende + -lich, a formation the page itself compares to English endly; Ende is the documented twin of end. [wiktionary]

leicht.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *linhtaz — English light is the explicit cognate: gh ↔ ch. [wiktionary]

richten.context_phrase: Richte die Bilder an der Wand.
richten.context_translation: Straighten the pictures on the wall.
richten.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *rihtijan (to right) — English right is the documented cognate; the gh that went silent in English still sounds as ch in German. [wiktionary]

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved the consonant as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Old English had /j/ and /x/ which became silent or vocalized. German kept sagen, Tag, gestern, Nacht, lachen, and Licht.
y_gh_to_g_ch.literature_source: Explains why English spelling has silent "gh" letters — they were original German-like gutturals!
